options.content:
### Response performance, read against usage pressure

Two questions that are only useful together: **is this service answering
quickly**, and **is the pipe under it busy**. The pair is cross-linked — every
panel here can hand you to
[Mesh Bandwidth Attribution](/d/mesh-bandwidth-attribution) on the same host over the same window,
and it links back.

**Read it as a quadrant.** That is the whole point of pairing them:

| | pipe quiet | pipe busy |
|---|---|---|
| **fast** | healthy | coping — headroom is real |
| **slow** | **the SERVICE is the problem** — the network is not your answer | **contention** — go to the bandwidth dashboard and find the category |

Correlation is not causation, and this dashboard does not claim it. It puts the
two facts on one screen with a shared time axis so the quadrant is readable;
deciding which way the arrow points is still yours.

**Latency here is Traefik's** — it is measured at the ingress and knows nothing
about how the client reached the mesh. The p2p-vs-relayed split below is a
*separate* measurement of the path, from `netbird status`. Do not read one as
the cause of the other without checking the third block.

Not every service, deliberately. Of the routers Traefik knows, only a handful
carry any traffic; the rest return `NaN` from `histogram_quantile` because
their buckets are empty. A dashboard that renders those as `0 s` would claim
every idle service is infinitely fast.

`$service` defaults to the set that actually moves requests. Widen it with the
picker — an idle service will show **No data**, which is the honest answer.

panels.title: Long-lived streams — measured as streams, not as requests

options.content:
**A stream's lifetime is not a response time.** `signal@file|portal@file` is the NetBird
signal server: it holds a gRPC stream open per peer, and Traefik times a stream
from open to close. A peer connected for twenty minutes is recorded as one
1200-second "request".

Measured here on 2026-08-14: **95.8% of signal requests finished under 100 ms**,
and 42 of 21,093 exceeded 5 s. That bimodal shape is quick RPCs plus a handful
of streams — not a slow service. Averaged together it dragged p99 to the
histogram ceiling and this dashboard reported the signal server as slow when it
is fast. Streaming services are now excluded from every percentile above.

What actually matters for a stream is **how many are open and how long they
last**, which is what these panels show. Note the bucket resolution is coarse
(Traefik's defaults are 0.1 / 0.3 / 1.2 / 5 s), so anything past 5 s is
"longer than 5 s" and nothing finer — appropriate for a stream, useless as a
latency figure.

panels.title: Stream completions by duration bucket
panels.description: Cumulative histogram buckets. The gap between the 5s line and +Inf is the genuinely long-lived streams — peers that stayed connected. Rising +Inf means more peers holding sessions, which is health, not latency.

panels.title: Streams opened/s
panels.description: Includes the quick RPCs on the same service — Traefik cannot separate them by route, so read this as signal-plane activity, not as sessions.

panels.title: Sessions lasting >5s (10m)
panels.description: The long tail, counted rather than averaged. THIS is the stream population; it was previously being reported as a 5-second p99.

panels.title: Signal errors (5xx)
panels.description: Failures ARE meaningful for a stream — this is the honest health signal for the signal plane, where latency is not.

panels.title: Open connections (all entrypoints)
panels.description: Concurrency across the edge. Streams are a concurrency cost, not a throughput cost — this is the number that grows with viewers.

panels.title: Fast-vs-stream split for stream-carrying services
panels.description: Share of this service's requests that completed under 1.2s — i.e. were ordinary requests rather than held-open streams. THIS is the page latency signal for a service whose percentile is unusable. A high share with a bad percentile means the pages are fine and the streams are just long, which is what a stream is supposed to be.

options.content:
**Why these services are excluded from the percentiles above**

Measured on 2026-08-14 over 30 minutes:

| service | evidence | reading |
|---|---|---|
| `signal` | 95.8% under 100 ms; 42 of 21,093 over 5 s | quick RPCs plus a few long gRPC streams |
| `portal` | **361 of 513 over 5 s (70%)** | the SSE route is the majority of what Traefik counts |

Traefik measures a stream open-to-close, so a peer connected for twenty minutes
is one 1200-second "request". Leaving these in reported the signal server as
slow when 95.8% of its work finishes in under a tenth of a second.

**This is a measurement limit, not a service verdict.** Router-label metrics
would let the SSE route be excluded on its own instead of the whole service —
`--metrics.prometheus.addRoutersLabels=true`, at the cost of a label per router.

**Where a client sits changes what "slow" means.** A relayed peer's traffic
goes node → relay → peer, so it carries the relay's round trip and the relay's
queue; a direct peer does not. Judging a service's response time without
knowing the path mix is judging two different populations as one.

This is measured by `netbird`, not by Traefik — it is the *path*, not the
service. **Only peers netbird has actually timed are counted.** It reports
`0` for peers it has not measured, and a 0 here would render as an
instantaneous link, so `goat_net_peer_latency_measured` gates every panel
below and the coverage tile says how much of the fleet is behind the number.

options.content:
**Two panels, one time axis, never one chart.** Latency and throughput have
different units and different scales; putting them on a shared y-axis (or worse,
two y-axes) invents a relationship by choosing where the lines cross. Stacked
panels let you read the same instant on both without the chart asserting
anything.

If the top line rises where the bottom line rises, that is worth investigating —
click through to
[Mesh Bandwidth Attribution](/d/mesh-bandwidth-attribution) with this window preserved and find
which category was consuming the pipe.

panels.title: Response by pressure band
panels.description: A crude banding: p99 restricted to windows where the link was moving bytes. It is deliberately crude — a real pressure/latency regression wants a load test (ADR 1012), not an observational join. This says 'look closer', never 'proven'.

targets.legendFormat: p99 while the link is carrying traffic

options.content:
**What this pair cannot tell you.**

- Traefik's latency is measured *at the ingress*. It does not include the
  client's mesh path, so a relayed client's felt latency is this number **plus**
  the relay hop in the block above.
- Jitter and packet loss are **not measured on this goatnet** —
  `goat_mesh_rtt_jitter_ms` and `goat_mesh_packet_loss_ratio` exist in the
  rules but the path-quality prober is not deployed here, so there are zero
  series. They are absent rather than shown as zero.
- Correlation on observed traffic is suggestive only. To establish that
  pressure *causes* latency, drive it: `zenoh-loadtest.md` / ADR 1012.

panels.title: Wire savings by client class
panels.description: Fraction of bytes compression removed, split by who the client is. READ THE `mesh` LINE — that is real users, and it ran 71-81% when goat-compress shipped. `gateway` is our own blackbox canary, which never sends Accept-Encoding and sits near zero (slightly negative, the honest cost of negotiation overhead on responses it cannot compress). A combined ratio would average these two into a number that means nothing.

panels.title: Origin vs wire bytes — real clients only
panels.description: The gap between these two lines IS the compression. Note this cannot be built from traefik_service_responses_bytes_total: that counter reports the origin figure only and is blind to compression, which is why this dashboard reads goat_traefik_* from the access log instead.

panels.title: Savings by service — real clients
panels.description: Per-surface compression. A surface dropping to zero here while others hold means its own route stopped matching the entrypoint middleware, not that compression fell over fleet-wide.

panels.title: Bytes left on the table
panels.description: Compressible content sent uncompressed because the client did not negotiate. On `gateway` this is expected and inert — the blackbox canary will never ask for gzip. On `mesh` it is actionable: a real client is paying for bytes it could have avoided. Reads 0 until the access log carries the response Content-Type (--accesslog.fields.headers.names.Content-Type=keep).

panels.title: Exporter health
panels.description: If this reads 0 the compression panels above are FROZEN at their last good values, not showing a real decline. The exporter carries counters forward on failure precisely so a broken reader cannot masquerade as broken compression.
